narrative.h2: Punk video keeps the camera honest by leaving it bruised

sections.heading: What punk looks like
sections.body: Punk MVs reject polish on principle. Handheld, often shot on whatever camera was nearby, frequently in a real venue with a real crowd. Lighting is whatever the venue had. The band plays full-volume; the camera operator clearly didn't sleep enough. Cuts are jagged, sometimes single-frame intercuts of static or text. The crowd is part of the frame, often the main subject. There's no separation between performer and audience — that distinction is the thing punk videos are trying to break.

sections.heading: Reference points that actually work
sections.body: IDLES' 'Mr. Motivator' is the modern template — band energy, color, no pretension. Turnstile's 'Holiday' and the full 'Glow On' run, directed by member Brendan Yates with Ian Hurdle, show how to make hardcore look beautiful without softening it. Fontaines DC's 'Big' brings the post-punk poetic lineage into the current vocabulary. Earlier markers — Nirvana's 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' directed by Samuel Bayer, The Clash's 'London Calling' shoots by Pennie Smith, and Liam Lynch's later live work with the Foo Fighters — still define what a real pit on camera should look like. The grammar: no clean takes.

sections.heading: Prompting tip for Tunee
sections.body: Specify the venue size. 'Hundred-capacity basement room, sweat condensing on the low ceiling, stage barely raised six inches' gives Tunee the right scale. Crowd should be in nearly every chorus frame, blurred bodies in the foreground. Avoid asking for clean focus or even framing — 'handheld, missed focus, occasional crowd member knocks the lens' is a real prompt that works. Cut on the snare hit, never the downbeat. Punk lives in the second beat, not the first.
